ai.definition: Emerging compute paradigms refer to novel computational approaches that aim to surpass the limitations of traditional, or 'classical', computer chips. These include neuromorphic and photonic computing technologies.
ai.howItWorks: These emerging technologies utilize unique substrates and mechanisms for processing information more efficiently than classical chips. Neuromorphic computing mimics the structure and function of biological neural networks to perform complex tasks with reduced energy consumption, while photonic computing leverages light-based components to significantly increase data processing speeds and reduce power consumption.
ai.problemSolved: They address the limitations of classical computing in terms of energy efficiency, speed, and scalability. Classical chips are reaching their physical limits, making it difficult to continue improving performance without increasing energy usage or size.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing these technologies is complex due to the need for specialized materials and processes. Neuromorphic devices often require advanced semiconductor fabrication techniques, while photonic components necessitate precise control over light-based structures such as waveguides and modulators.
ai.buildProcess: The build process involves creating intricate circuits at a microscopic scale using techniques like lithography and etching. For neuromorphic computing, this includes integrating artificial neural network architectures into silicon chips. Photonic computing requires the creation of optical components that can handle high-speed data transmission and processing.
ai.costDrivers: High initial investment in research and development, specialized equipment, and materials are significant cost drivers. The need for advanced fabrication facilities and skilled labor also contributes to higher costs.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The outlook is promising but faces challenges in widespread adoption due to technical hurdles and the need for standardization.
ai.regulation: Regulatory frameworks are still being developed, particularly concerning data security and privacy issues associated with neuromorphic computing's ability to process information more closely resembling biological neural networks.
ai.risks: Technical risks include reliability concerns and the potential for increased heat generation. Market risks involve competition from established chip manufacturers and the need for significant investment in new infrastructure.
ai.profitability: Profitability is uncertain due to high development costs, but there are opportunities for early adopters in specific applications such as AI and data centers.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future developments will likely focus on improving energy efficiency, increasing integration with classical computing systems, and expanding application areas beyond specialized niches.

glossary.def: A computational paradigm inspired by the structure and function of biological neural networks.
A form of computing that uses light instead of electrical signals to process information, aiming for faster processing speeds and lower energy consumption.

subsystems.name: Device layer
subsystems.role: the physical units that imitate neurons and synapses, or that manipulate light instead of electrons.

subsystems.name: Weight storage
subsystems.role: holds the model's parameters where the computation happens, avoiding shuttling data to and from memory.

subsystems.name: Light sources and detectors
subsystems.role: supply and read the optical signals in photonic designs.

subsystems.name: Interconnect and packaging
subsystems.role: moves signals between chips and to the outside world.

subsystems.name: Analog support circuitry
subsystems.role: bridges the analog or optical core to ordinary digital systems.

subsystems.name: Software stack
subsystems.role: compiles trained networks onto hardware that does not behave like a normal CPU.

buildSteps.title: Design at device level
buildSteps.detail: The network is expressed as events for spiking hardware, or as matrices mapped onto interferometers or crossbar rows and columns.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate the CMOS base
buildSteps.detail: Control logic and neuron circuits are made in a standard silicon foundry on mature nodes, which keeps cost down.

buildSteps.title: Add the special layer
buildSteps.detail: Photonic waveguides, modulators and detectors are patterned in the same flow, or resistive memory cells are built into the wiring layers above the transistors.

buildSteps.title: Attach light sources
buildSteps.detail: Because silicon does not emit light well, III-V laser material is bonded or micro-transfer-printed onto the chip and aligned to the waveguides.

buildSteps.title: Package and cool
buildSteps.detail: Fibres are coupled to the chip edges with sub-micron alignment, and the package is built to hold temperature stable because optical and analog behaviour drifts with heat.

buildSteps.title: Calibrate
buildSteps.detail: Every device is slightly different, so phase shifters, laser power and resistance levels are tuned individually before use.

buildSteps.title: Compile or train
buildSteps.detail: A trained model is mapped onto the hardware, or the chip is trained in place by adjusting its physical weights.

buildSteps.title: Deploy in a niche
buildSteps.detail: The first uses are where the advantage is clearest: always-on sensing, event-based vision and low-power inference at the edge.

prerequisites.why: optical transceivers already ship in volume, giving a supply chain for waveguides and modulators.
moving optics next to the processor is the step that makes photonic computing practical.
memristors and phase-change cells drift and vary, which limits accuracy without heavy calibration.

prerequisites.tech: Mature spiking software and training methods
prerequisites.why: ordinary deep-learning tools assume dense arithmetic, not sparse spikes or analog physics.
optical computing needs light on the chip without large external laser racks.

pathway.milestone: research chips such as IBM's TrueNorth, Intel's Loihi and the SpiNNaker systems, plus event-based vision sensors
pathway.unlocks: proven low-power, event-driven computation in the lab.

pathway.milestone: photonic interconnects and co-packaged optics in datacentres
pathway.unlocks: a manufacturing base and design tools for chips that compute with light.

pathway.milestone: hybrid accelerators that do matrix multiplication optically or in analog memory, with digital cleanup
pathway.unlocks: big energy savings for inference-heavy workloads such as AI models.

pathway.milestone: brain-scale spiking systems and in-situ learning on edge devices
pathway.unlocks: always-on sensing and robotics that cannot afford to run conventional chips.
